claim: Before the COVID-19 pandemic began, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was among the top priorities for global public health.
source: Before the coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic began, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was among the top priorities for global public health.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a contextual statement about AMR's priority status before COVID-19.

claim: The COVID-19 outbreak was declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization (WHO) on 11 March 2020.
source: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, was declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization (WHO) on 11 March 2020 (Ghebreyesus, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ghebreyesus, 2020.

claim: AMR had been named a priority for global public health for the year 2020.
source: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a similarly cross-sectoral challenge which has received increased international attention since 2015 (WHO, 2015a), had already been named a priority for global public health for the year 2020 (World Health Organization, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to WHO, 2015a and World Health Organization, 2020.

claim: There were 182,000 deaths from multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) in 2019.
source: Based on previous estimates of the number of deaths from multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) alone (182,000 in 2019; WHO, 2020d)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020d.

claim: MDR-TB is thought to contribute a third of the AMR burden.
source: thought to contribute a third of the burden (Global Fund, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Global Fund, 2019.

claim: AMR is likely to have caused a third as many deaths as COVID-19 in 2020 (1.8 million).
source: AMR is likely to have caused a third as many deaths as COVID-19 in 2020 (1.8 million; WHO, 2020h).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from MDR-TB deaths and COVID-19 deaths, with citation to WHO, 2020h for COVID-19 deaths.

claim: COVID-19 symptoms can resemble bacterial pneumonia.
source: First, COVID-19 symptoms can resemble bacterial pneumonia.
evidence: This is stated as a reason why patients with COVID-19 may receive antimicrobial therapy.

claim: C-reactive protein, a biomarker that is elevated in bacterial infections but typically not in viral ones, may in fact be increased in patients with COVID-19.
source: For example, faster tests, such as diagnostics measuring C-reactive protein – a biomarker that is elevated in bacterial infections but typically not in viral ones – may in fact be increased in patients with COVID-19 (Sproston and Ashworth, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sproston and Ashworth, 2018.

claim: Many patients hospitalised with COVID-19 will be prescribed empiric antibiotics, often in the absence of a microbiological confirmation of the diagnosis.
source: As a result, many patients hospitalised with COVID-19 will be prescribed empiric antibiotics, often in the absence of a microbiological confirmation of the diagnosis (Langford et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Langford et al., 2021.

claim: Secondary bacterial infection rates in COVID-19 patients are low (<20%).
source: Several evidence reviews suggest that the secondary bacterial infection rates are low (<20%) (Langford et al., 2020; Lansbury et al., 2020; Rawson et al., 2020b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple evidence reviews.

claim: Inappropriate treatment in either direction has been associated with increased risk of mortality.
source: Inappropriate treatment in either direction has been associated with increased risk of mortality (Gutiérrez-Gutiérrez et al., 2017; Paul et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gutiérrez-Gutiérrez et al., 2017 and Paul et al., 2010.

claim: In areas where carbapenem resistance is high, antibiotics with less favourable safety profiles such as colistin may be recommended as a first-line treatment for suspected Gram-negative infections.
source: For example, in areas where carbapenem resistance is high, antibiotics with less favourable safety profiles such as colistin may be recommended as a first-line treatment for suspected Gram-negative infections (Torres et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Torres et al., 2017.

claim: The evolution of AMR in a population is determined by three components: emergence, transmission, and population-level infection burden.
source: The evolution of AMR in a population is determined by three components: emergence-, transmission-, and population-level infection burden.
evidence: This is stated as a framework for understanding AMR evolution.

claim: AMR emergence can be driven by selective pressures on microbial populations within humans, animals, or in the environment.
source: AMR emergence can be driven by selective pressures on microbial populations within humans, animals, or in the environment.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism of AMR emergence.

claim: Selective pressures facilitate resistance acquisition mechanisms such as point mutation or horizontal transfer of genes encoding resistance to one or several antibiotics.
source: Subject to the 'drug and bug' of concern, such selective pressures facilitate resistance acquisition mechanisms such as point mutation or horizontal transfer of genes encoding resistance to one or several antibiotics (Davies and Davies, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies and Davies, 2010.

claim: Environmental conditions and behaviours may enable or prevent transmission of antimicrobial-resistant organisms (AROs) between humans, animals, and environments.
source: Environmental conditions and behaviours may subsequently enable or prevent transmission of these emerged antimicrobial-resistant organisms (AROs) between humans, animals, and environments (Robinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robinson et al., 2016.

claim: As many as 70% of patients with COVID-19 receive antimicrobials either in the outpatient or inpatient setting.
source: As many as 70% of patients with COVID-19 receive antimicrobials either in the outpatient or inpatient setting (ISARIC, 2020; Langford et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ISARIC, 2020 and Langford et al., 2021.

claim: The pandemic may result in a large cohort of COVID-19 survivors with residual post-COVID-19 chronic lung disease (such as interstitial lung disease and bronchiectasis) who will be at risk of acute exacerbations.
source: It is also likely that the pandemic may result in a large cohort of COVID-19 survivors with residual post-COVID-19 chronic lung disease (such as interstitial lung disease and bronchiectasis) who will be at risk of acute exacerbations (George et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to George et al., 2020.

claim: Extensive lung damage has been reported on high-resolution chest computed-tomography several weeks into COVID-19 illness.
source: Long-term sequelae of individuals recovered from moderate to severe COVID-19 is currently unknown, but extensive lung damage has been reported on high-resolution chest computed -tomography several weeks into the illness (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: In patients with post-COVID-19 structural lung damage, frequent courses of antibiotics and hospital admissions may lead to increased risk of colonisation and infection with resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: In patients with post-COVID-19 structural lung damage, frequent courses of antibiotics and hospital admissions may lead to increased risk of colonisation and infection with resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Rodrigo-Troyano and Sibila, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rodrigo-Troyano and Sibila, 2017.

claim: There is mounting evidence of a lack of efficacy of chloroquine for treating COVID-19.
source: For example, despite mounting evidence of a lack of efficacy (Kashour et al., 2021; UKRI, 2020; WHO, 2020e), the antimalarial drug chloroquine has been used to treat COVID-19.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kashour et al., 2021; UKRI, 2020; WHO, 2020e.

claim: Chloroquine remains the drug of choice for malaria in high non-Plasmodium falciparum prevalence malaria settings.
source: This is of particular concern in high non-Plasmodium falciparum prevalence malaria settings, where chloroquine remains the drug of choice for malaria (WHO, 2015b)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2015b.

claim: COVID-19 symptoms could be mistaken for other diseases such as malaria or tuberculosis (TB), and vice versa.
source: Because a patient with COVID-19 can present with non-specific symptoms (e.g. fever and/or persistent cough), these could be mistaken for other disease such as malaria (Chanda-Kapata et al., 2020) or tuberculosis (TB) (The Lancet Hiv, 2020), and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chanda-Kapata et al., 2020 and The Lancet Hiv, 2020.

claim: The widespread use of azithromycin for WHO-recommended mass drug administration campaigns for trachoma has resulted in bystander selection.
source: The importance of such bystander selection has already been seen following the widespread use of azithromycin for WHO-recommended mass drug administration campaigns for trachoma (O'Brien et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Brien et al., 2019.

claim: The initial use of hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin for COVID-19 has now been halted in some settings (e.g. in the US).
source: As the evidence mounts on the lack of efficacy of hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin for treatment of COVID-19, their initial use has now been halted in some settings (e.g. in the US [Acosta et al., 2020; Bull-Otterson et al., 2020; Kadri et al., 2020]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acosta et al., 2020; Bull-Otterson et al., 2020; Kadri et al., 2020.

claim: In many African countries, despite WHO recommendations, hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin were still being advised for use in the summer of 2020.
source: For example, in many African countries, despite WHO recommendations, hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and azithromycin were still being advised for use in the summer of 2020 and may be still being used off-label (Abena et al., 2020; Belayneh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abena et al., 2020 and Belayneh, 2020.

claim: In India, it appears to still be guidance to use hydroxychloroquine as a prophylactic for 'healthcare workers'.
source: In India, it appears to still be guidance to use hydroxychloroquine as a prophylactic for 'healthcare workers' (National Taskforce for COVID-19, India, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to National Taskforce for COVID-19, India, 2020.

claim: Cheap, rapid tests may detect SARS-CoV-2 infections earlier and hence prevent some antibiotic use.
source: In community settings, cheap, rapid tests may detect SARS-CoV-2 infections earlier (Mina et al., 2020), especially in the face of unspecific symptoms, and hence prevent some antibiotic use.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mina et al., 2020 and involves inference about the impact on antibiotic use.

claim: Some current diagnostics for asymptomatic testing in the community, such as lateral flow tests, remain insensitive and risk providing 'false negatives' with a sense of security that is not accurate.
source: Moreover, some current diagnostics for asymptomatic testing in the community, such as lateral flow tests, remain insensitive and risk providing 'false negatives' with a sense of security that is not accurate (Mahase, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mahase, 2020.

claim: Prolonged changes in antimicrobial use in humans during the COVID-19 crisis could mean increased antimicrobial production, which may accelerate changes in antimicrobial concentrations in the environment.
source: If prolonged, changes in antimicrobial use in humans during the COVID-19 crisis could mean increased antimicrobial production, which may accelerate changes in antimicrobial concentrations in the environment and, consequently, affect selective pressures for AMR in water and soil systems (WHO, 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020a and involves speculation about future impacts.

claim: Disruption within a single Chinese factory resulted in an international shortage of piperacillin-tazobactam.
source: The fragility of the antibiotic pipeline was highlighted recently when disruption within a single Chinese factory resulted in an international shortage of piperacillin-tazobactam (Davis, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis, 2017.

claim: In some countries, such as the UK, 80–90% of generic medicines are imported.
source: In some countries, such as the UK, 80–90% of generic medicines are imported (Business and Energy and Industrial Strategy Committee, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Business and Energy and Industrial Strategy Committee, 2018.

claim: Most countries are net importers of antibiotics.
source: Indeed, most countries are net importers of antibiotics (Simoes and Hidalgo, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Simoes and Hidalgo, 2011.

claim: Countries that manufacture and export antibiotics are facing increased home market demands due to COVID-19 which may lead to a reduction in exports, as seen in India.
source: Countries that manufacture and export antibiotics are facing increased home market demands due to COVID-19 which may lead to a reduction in exports, as seen in India (Government of India, 2020; Guerin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Government of India, 2020 and Guerin et al., 2020.

claim: 10 manufacturers have reported shortages of azithromycin to the US Food and Drug Administration, potentially because of its use for COVID-19 treatment.
source: As COVID-19 is also likely to lead to changes in the use of antibiotics, this will have a similar effect on supply chain shortages; 10 manufacturers have reported shortages of azithromycin to the US Food and Drug Administration, potentially because of its use for COVID-19 treatment (US Food and Drug Administration, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to US Food and Drug Administration, 2020.

claim: Low- and middle-income country (LMIC) settings are particularly vulnerable to supply chain issues where weak health systems and poor quality control of medicines are barriers to antimicrobial access.
source: Low- and middle-income country (LMIC) settings are particularly vulnerable to supply chain issues where weak health systems and poor quality control of medicines are barriers to antimicrobial access (Frost et al., 2019; Laxminarayan et al., 2016; Pokharel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frost et al., 2019; Laxminarayan et al., 2016; Pokharel et al., 2019.

claim: Uneven supplies of different antimicrobials across all income settings raise concerns about AMR emergence due to suboptimal antibiotic use.
source: Uneven supplies of different antimicrobials across all income settings (Pauwels et al., 2015; Tickell et al., 2019) raise concerns about AMR emergence due to suboptimal antibiotic use (Access to Medicine Foundation, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pauwels et al., 2015; Tickell et al., 2019; Access to Medicine Foundation, 2018.

claim: Substandard or counterfeit drugs may not only be the inappropriate choice for the illness but may have suboptimal concentrations of antimicrobial, favouring resistance, and can potentially be toxic to the patients.
source: Such medicines may not only be the inappropriate choice for the illness but may have suboptimal concentrations of antimicrobial, favouring resistance, and can potentially be toxic to the patients (Kelesidis and Falagas, 2015; Pisani, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kelesidis and Falagas, 2015 and Pisani, 2015.

claim: In the case of TB, which requires prolonged multidrug therapy, one consequence of drug shortages will be short-term treatment interruptions potentially leading to increased risk of treatment failure and development of resistance.
source: In the case of TB, which requires prolonged multidrug therapy, one consequence of drug shortages will be short-term treatment interruptions potentially leading to increased risk of treatment failure and development of resistance (Adepoju, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adepoju, 2020.

claim: A reduction in income has been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland.
source: In high-income country (HIC) settings, where prescriptions for antibiotics are required, it is likely that a reduction in income will be associated with poorer health; such reductions have previously been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland (Covvey et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Covvey et al., 2014.

claim: A reduction in income has been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Sweden.
source: such reductions have previously been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland (Covvey et al., 2014), Sweden (Nilsson and Laurell, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nilsson and Laurell, 2005.

claim: A reduction in income has been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in the US.
source: such reductions have previously been associated with higher rates of both respiratory infections and antibiotic prescribing in Scotland (Covvey et al., 2014), Sweden (Nilsson and Laurell, 2005), and, more recently, in the US (Kissler et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kissler et al., 2020.

claim: Less prosperous socioeconomic areas within countries have experienced a higher burden of COVID-19.
source: Similarly, less prosperous socioeconomic areas within such countries have experienced a higher burden of COVID-19 (Ahmed et al., 2020; Office for National Statistics, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2020 and Office for National Statistics, 2020.

claim: Financial shocks due to COVID-19 policies may increase the need for people to use over-the-counter services including for unregulated antimicrobials in an attempt to reduce healthcare expenditure in LMIC settings.
source: In LMIC settings, where there is already less regulation of antimicrobial purchasing, the financial shocks due to COVID-19 policies may increase the need for people to use over-the-counter services including for unregulated antimicrobials in an attempt to reduce healthcare expenditure (Frost et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Frost et al., 2019 and involves speculation about future behavior.

claim: Subtherapeutic doses of drugs and shortened courses of antimicrobials have been associated with increased mortality.
source: This presents a higher risk of subtherapeutic doses of drugs and shortened courses of antimicrobials, as well as increased mortality (Laxminarayan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laxminarayan et al., 2013.

claim: Health systems that already struggle to provide sufficient access to antimicrobials may face further challenges to deliver due to the economic reverberations of the COVID-19 crisis.
source: On the other hand, the economic reverberations of this crisis mean that health systems that already struggle to provide sufficient access to antimicrobials (Frost et al., 2019; Laxminarayan et al., 2016) may face further challenges to deliver
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frost et al., 2019 and Laxminarayan et al., 2016, and involves inference about future impacts.

claim: Access to medicines has been shown to correlate with higher burden of preventable infections such as community-acquired pneumonia in children under 5.
source: This may result in a potential increase in mortality, while such access has been shown to correlate with higher burden of preventable infections such as community-acquired pneumonia in children under 5 (Laxminarayan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laxminarayan et al., 2016.

claim: Gender inequalities impact both COVID-19 and AMR due to the uneven distribution of infectious disease prevalence and burden.
source: For example, gender inequalities impact both COVID-19 and AMR due to the uneven distribution of infectious disease prevalence and burden (Horton et al., 2016; McQuaid et al., 2020; Schröder et al., 2016; Wenham et al., 2020; Zanichelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horton et al., 2016; McQuaid et al., 2020; Schröder et al., 2016; Wenham et al., 2020; Zanichelli et al., 2019.

claim: Black, Asian, and minority ethnic (BAME) populations suffer from both a greater economic impact and worse health outcomes from COVID-19.
source: The pandemic has also highlighted racial inequality; in particular, the Black, Asian, and minority ethnic (BAME) categorisation has been used in some countries (Hu, 2020) to show how these populations suffer from both a greater economic impact and worse health outcomes from COVID-19 (Public Health England, 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hu, 2020 and Public Health England, 2020a.

claim: In the UK, BAME populations have higher rates of circulating AMR in the community.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that in the UK BAME populations also have higher rates of circulating AMR in the community (Lishman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lishman et al., 2016.

claim: Countries with the greatest AMR burden are those in which spread of pathogens, rather than overuse of antimicrobials, is the dominant factor.
source: It has been postulated that countries with the greatest AMR burden are those in which spread of pathogens, rather than overuse of antimicrobials, is the dominant factor (Collignon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Collignon et al., 2018.

claim: For MDR-TB, the majority of cases result from transmission events rather than acquisition of spontaneous resistance emerging during treatment.
source: For MDR-TB – the largest single disease component of the global AMR burden (The Review on Antimicrobial Resistance, 2016) – the majority of cases result from transmission events rather than acquisition of spontaneous resistance emerging during treatment (Kendall et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to The Review on Antimicrobial Resistance, 2016 and Kendall et al., 2015.

claim: Patients with severe COVID-19 may be hospitalised for prolonged periods of time.
source: Patients with severe COVID-19 may be hospitalised for prolonged periods of time (Rees et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rees et al., 2020.

claim: Patients hospitalised for prolonged periods of time are at high risk for acquiring nosocomial infections.
source: Patients with severe COVID-19 may be hospitalised for prolonged periods of time (Rees et al., 2020), and hence are at high risk for acquiring nosocomial infections (Asensio et al., 1996; Oztoprak et al., 2006; Wolkewitz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Asensio et al., 1996; Oztoprak et al., 2006; Wolkewitz et al., 2008.

claim: Early anecdotal evidence from two acute care facilities in New York and Missouri reported three- to fourfold increases in central line-associated bloodstream infection rates, likely related to a shift towards a higher risk case-mix.
source: Early anecdotal evidence from two acute care facilities in New York and Missouri reported three- to fourfold increases in central line-associated bloodstream infection rates, likely related to a shift towards a higher risk case-mix (McMullen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McMullen et al., 2020.

claim: The hardships and resource strains due to COVID-19 have affected antimicrobial stewardship activities.
source: The hardships and resource strains due to COVID-19 have also affected antimicrobial stewardship activities (Hsu, 2020; De Waele et al., 2021; Ginsburg and Klugman, 2020; Lynch et al., 2020; Seaton, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hsu, 2020; De Waele et al., 2021; Ginsburg and Klugman, 2020; Lynch et al., 2020; Seaton, 2020.

claim: Antimicrobial stewardship programmes in hospitals have the potential to significantly reduce incidence of infections with ARO.
source: It is known that antimicrobial stewardship programmes in hospitals have the potential to significantly reduce incidence of infections with ARO (Baur et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baur et al., 2017.

claim: Increased acquisition of MRSA occurred during the SARS outbreak in 2003 in an intensive care unit in China.
source: Some of these factors likely contributed to an increased acquisition of MRSA during the SARS outbreak in 2003 in an intensive care unit in China (Yap et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yap et al., 2004.

claim: Handwashing alone could prevent 30% of diarrhoeal episodes in LMICs.
source: Studies have shown that handwashing alone could prevent 30% of diarrhoeal episodes in LMICs (Ejemot-Nwadiaro et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ejemot-Nwadiaro et al., 2015.

claim: Up to 50% of children with diarrhoea in LMICs receive antibiotics.
source: As a result, increased hand hygiene to prevent SARS-CoV-2 transmission could reduce diarrhoeal incidence and hence the high number of antibiotic courses given to children with diarrhoea in LMICs (up to 50% with diarrhoea receive antibiotics) (Fink et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fink et al., 2020.

claim: Low-level use of biocides can select for resistance both to the biocides and to antimicrobials.
source: It has been shown that low-level use of these agents can select for resistance both to the biocides and to antimicrobials (Caselli, 2017; Hardy et al., 2018; Hora et al., 2020; Kampf, 2018; Maillard et al., 2020; McCarlie et al., 2020; Wales and Davies, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caselli, 2017; Hardy et al., 2018; Hora et al., 2020; Kampf, 2018; Maillard et al., 2020; McCarlie et al., 2020; Wales and Davies, 2015.

claim: Numbers of invasive bacterial infections appear to have decreased in 2020.
source: For example, numbers of invasive bacterial infections appear to have decreased in 2020 (Brueggemann et al., 2020), such as Invasive Group A Streptococcal Infections in the UK (Public Health England, 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brueggemann et al., 2020 and Public Health England, 2020a.

claim: Many settings have seen far reduced influenza infection levels.
source: Similarly, many settings have seen far reduced influenza infection levels (WHO, 2020n)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020n.

claim: Prolonged time at home due to COVID-19 interventions could result in increased transmission of other pathogens between household members.
source: Within a household setting, prolonged time at home due to COVID-19 interventions could result in increased transmission of other pathogens between household members (Maillard et al., 2020) (e.g. of MRSA [Mollema et al., 2010], Streptococcus pneumoniae [Althouse et al., 2017], and MDR-TB [Grandjean et al., 2015; Leung et al., 2013; Paul and Kollikkara, 2014])
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maillard et al., 2020; Mollema et al., 2010; Althouse et al., 2017; Grandjean et al., 2015; Leung et al., 2013; Paul and Kollikkara, 2014.

claim: MDR-TB usually only has 10% of transmission occurring within the home and is likely saturating.
source: Alternatively, MDR-TB, a disease also caused by a respiratory pathogen, usually only has 10% of transmission occurring within the home and is likely saturating (Glynn et al., 2015; McCreesh and White, 2018; Middelkoop et al., 2015; Verver et al., 2004; Wilkinson et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Glynn et al., 2015; McCreesh and White, 2018; Middelkoop et al., 2015; Verver et al., 2004; Wilkinson et al., 1997.

claim: Following travel to countries with high AMR prevalence, travellers can return colonised with bacteria carrying AMR genes and remain colonised for substantial periods of time.
source: For example, it is known that following travel to countries with high AMR prevalence, travellers can return colonised with bacteria carrying AMR genes and remain colonised for substantial periods of time (Arcilla et al., 2017; ÖstholmBalkhed et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arcilla et al., 2017 and ÖstholmBalkhed et al., 2018.

claim: Approximately three-quarters of programmes and service deliveries for HIV, TB, and malaria have been disrupted as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Approximately three-quarters of programmes and service deliveries for HIV, TB, and malaria have been disrupted as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic (Fund, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fund, 2020.

claim: South Africa and China have experienced large reductions in TB and MDR-TB testing in the first period of 2020.
source: For example, South Africa and China have experienced large reductions in TB and MDR-TB testing in the first period of 2020 (Liu et al., 2020; National Institute for Communicable Diseases, Centre for Tuberculosis, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020 and National Institute for Communicable Diseases, Centre for Tuberculosis, 2020.

claim: Successful treatment rates for patients with MDR-TB remain low at 56%.
source: Successful treatment rates for patients with MDR-TB remain low at 56% (WHO, 2020g)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020g.

claim: Clinical care disruption may lead to a total reduction in in-patient antibiotic prescribing despite high levels of use in those with COVID-19.
source: Clinical care disruption may lead to a total reduction in in-patient antibiotic prescribing despite high levels of use in those with COVID-19 (Clancy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clancy et al., 2020.

claim: Signs of a reduction in antibiotic use have been seen in healthcare settings in the US.
source: Signs of a reduction in use have been seen in healthcare settings in the US, but a concomitantly larger reduction in bed days has sometimes led to an increased number of days of therapy per occupied bed day (Buehrle et al., 2020; Dieringer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buehrle et al., 2020 and Dieringer et al., 2020.

claim: Prescription of antibiotics to patients with COVID-19 clashes with the key public health message that antibiotics do not work for viral infections.
source: The widely reported prescription of antibiotics to patients with COVID-19 clashes with the key public health message that antibiotics do not work for viral infections.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about conflicting public health messages.

claim: Following the 2009 influenza pandemic, patients in the community had greater expectations of receiving antibiotics for flu-like symptoms.
source: This could lead to patients in the community having greater expectations of receiving antibiotics for flu-like symptoms, as was the case following the 2009 influenza pandemic (McNulty et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McNulty et al., 2012.

claim: A potential signal of increased antibiotic prescribing has been seen in data from the UK.
source: A potential signal of this has been seen in data from the UK (Armitage and Nellums, 2020; MacKenna, 2020) and likely increased prescribing for dental care (Croser, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Armitage and Nellums, 2020; MacKenna, 2020; and Croser, 2020.

claim: In England there has been an up to 50% reduction in Accident and Emergency attendance in some regions.
source: For example, in England there has been an up to 50% reduction in Accident and Emergency attendance in some regions (NHS England, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to NHS England, 2020.

claim: In England there has been a 20% reduction in appointments.
source: For example, in England there has been an up to 50% reduction in Accident and Emergency attendance in some regions (NHS England, 2020) and a 20% reduction in appointments (Armitage and Nellums, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Armitage and Nellums, 2020.

claim: In the community in England, a reduction in prescriptions for some antibiotics has been seen, for example, for those used to treat skin and urinary tract infections (flucloxacillin and nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim).
source: In the community in England, a reduction in prescriptions for some antibiotics has been seen, for example, for those used to treat skin and urinary tract infections (flucloxacillin and nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim) (MacKenna, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacKenna, 2020.

claim: Due to the decrease in the total number of appointments in England, the number of antibiotic prescriptions was higher than expected.
source: but due to the decrease in the total number of appointments the number of antibiotic prescriptions was higher than expected (Armitage and Nellums, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Armitage and Nellums, 2020.

claim: The fear of attending clinical settings, alongside the disruption to routine immunisation activities due to COVID-19-related burden, has led to reductions in overall vaccination coverage globally.
source: The fear of attending clinical settings, alongside the disruption to routine immunisation activities due to COVID-19-related burden, has led to reductions in overall vaccination coverage globally (Bramer et al., 2020; McDonald et al., 2020; Saxena et al., 2020; WHO, 2020j).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bramer et al., 2020; McDonald et al., 2020; Saxena et al., 2020; WHO, 2020j.

claim: Vaccines are a key tool to prevent infections, and hence antibiotic use and associated resistance.
source: Vaccines are a key tool to prevent infections, and hence antibiotic use and associated resistance (Lipsitch and Siber, 2016; Malarski et al., 2019; ReAct, 2020; Sosler, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lipsitch and Siber, 2016; Malarski et al., 2019; ReAct, 2020; Sosler, 2020.

claim: Some vaccines specifically target resistant subpopulations, for example, serotypes of S. pneumoniae with higher resistance to penicillin.
